plaques.Q45585: The militia company of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq steps out of the courtyard and into light. Rembrandt turns a group portrait into action: spears, shadow, and one small girl in gold.
plaques.Q21726709: A brawl erupts in an inn bedroom. Figures crowd the little room: some fight, some pull back, some look on. After a trip to Holland in 1773, Defrance made a specialty of such scenes, translating seventeenth-century Dutch tavern painting into the language of his own century. This panel is the companion to Women Fighting; both are now in the State Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg.
plaques.Q20354498: Horses rear, pistols flash, and bodies already litter the foreground. To the right a stone tower and wall pin the fight in place; farther off, more cavalry press across the plain beneath a windmill and a sky of piled cloud. A drum, fallen hats, and discarded kit lie in the dirt like the residue of the last charge.Breydel did not paint a named siege. Collectors of his day wanted the look of war—dust, smoke, tangled riders—more than a chronicle of any one campaign. Trained in Antwerp and formed by the battle pictures of Adam Frans van der Meulen, he made a specialty of these compact cavalry clashes. The composition is built in layers: a dark, crowded foreground; a smoky middle distance; and a high, open sky that keeps the violence from swallowing the whole scene.Works of this kind were often painted as pairs. One signed example entered the Danish royal collection in the 1740s and remains in Copenhagen. The date 1713 places the picture in Breydel’s mature years, after his return from Germany and Amsterdam, when he was a master in Antwerp’s Guild of Saint Luke and the War of the Spanish Succession had made such subjects fashionable across Europe
plaques.Q221150: A young woman turns toward us against a dark ground. The pearl, the turban, and the half-open mouth are a tronie: a face study, not a named portrait.
plaques.Q34535770: The Massacre of the Innocents (Matthew 2:16–18) Hieronymus Francken III Antwerp, 1611–after 1661 1653 Oil on oak panel, 40.3 × 57 cm Soldiers seize the infant boys of Bethlehem on Herod’s order. Mothers resist; the dead already lie at their feet; a city of columns and a distant landscape hold the crowd in place. Francken, son of Frans Francken the Younger, painted in the family manner of small, many-figured histories, with fuller, more robust bodies than his father’s. The panel comes from the Electoral gallery of Mainz and is now in the Staatsgalerie, Schloss Johannisburg, Aschaffenburg.
plaques.Q49342385: Market Scene Hendrick van Steenwijck the Elder (Flemish, c. 1550–1603) ca. 1590 Oil on canvas 51 5/8 × 70 3/8 in. (131.1 × 178.8 cm) A crowded marketplace in a Low Countries port town. Van Steenwijck, better known for church interiors, uses the same architectural eye here: measured space, receding streets, and figures set into the square rather than dominating it. Gift of Emile Wolf. Yale University Art Gallery, 1990.57.1. Public domain.
plaques.Q21616953: Christ Driving the Money-changers from the Temple Theodoor Rombouts (Antwerp, 1597–1637) c. 1628 Oil on canvas 168 × 238.5 cm Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp Christ bursts into the Temple courts with a whip of cords, overturning tables and driving out the merchants and money-changers who have turned a house of prayer into a marketplace. The episode, told in all four Gospels, is captured at its most violent instant: figures recoil, coins scatter, animals bolt, and ledgers teeter on the edge of a counter.
plaques.Q120969568: The Court’s Departure for the Hunt from the Venaria Reale Melchior Hamers (Antwerp, 1638–1709/10) c. 1665 Oil on canvas 123 × 177.4 cm The Savoy court rides out from the hunting palace of Venaria. At the center, Duke Charles Emmanuel II (1634–1675) sits a white horse; pages, grooms, and hounds form a ceremonial procession. Behind them rise the seventeenth-century entrance, clock tower, and the bronze stag that crowned the gate. The hunt is shown as court ritual—an image of rank, order, and princely power—not a chase in the woods.
plaques.Q594406: The Fall of the Rebel Angels Pieter Bruegel the Elder (c. 1525/30–1569) 1562 Oil on oak panel 117 × 162 cm Archangel Michael, slim in gold armor, drives Lucifer and the rebel angels out of Heaven. As they fall from a burst of light at the top of the panel, they twist into hybrid monsters — part human, part insect, fish, shell, and machine. The upper half is Heaven; the lower half darkens into chaos. The subject comes from Revelation 12. Bruegel treats a familiar Christian story as a swarm of invention, closer to Bosch than to Italian history painting. Bruegel painted this in Antwerp in 1562, while he was still designing prints for Hieronymus Cock and before his move to Brussels.
plaques.Q21809315:
Ayne Bru does not stage a ceremonial beheading. He paints a butcher’s task. The executioner grimaces, grips the saint’s hair, and opens the throat with a short knife; spare blades sit in a basket at his feet. Blood runs onto the ground. Cucuphas’s body slumps against the tree, halo still in place. The three men in brocade and scarlet discuss the scene as if it were already over. The dog, famous later when Salvador Dalí quoted it, is the only figure that seems to notice the body.

Behind them the monastery appears not as legend but as architecture of Bru’s own day. The painting was made for that building, and it returns the building to the moment of the saint’s death. Violence and topography share one panel: a local martyrdom made exact enough to serve both altar and record.
plaques.Q19928826: Cornelis de Man Delft 1621–1706 Smack Hands (Handjeklap), 1671 Oil on canvas A group gathers in a modest interior to play handjeklap, a lively guessing game in which one player hides their face while others slap an open hand. The guesser must name the striker. De Man captures the moment of anticipation and laughter with the clear, even light and attentive observation of gesture and costume that characterize Delft genre painting of the 1660s and 1670s. The subject was popular among Dutch artists. In tavern or peasant settings it could suggest unrestrained merriment; here the figures remain relatively composed, typical of de Man’s quieter approach compared with more raucous scenes by Jan Steen or Adriaen van Ostade.
plaques.Q64538737: The Interior of the Colosseum The Colosseum is no longer a stadium. It is a cave of stone. Challe draws you into the ellipse itself: stacked arches, broken masonry, light falling through a wound in the roof. A few tiny figures, if they appear at all, exist only to measure the ruin. The building that once held fifty thousand spectators has become geology.
plaques.Q27011675: Portrait of Johanna Magdalena de Mey (1719–1783) A Rotterdam woman, painted at forty-one, looks out from a world of silk, lace, and civic duty. De la Croix does not invent drama. He records presence: a face trained for company, a body arranged for posterity. Two years earlier he had painted her father. This canvas completes the household in paint. Pierre Frédéric de la Croix was born in France in 1709 and became a Dutch painter by residence and guild. Deaf and mute, he worked in Amsterdam and The Hague, joined the Confrerie Pictura in 1753, and made his living in the most social of arts: portraiture.
plaques.Q27751303: The Immaculate Conception Mary does not stand on the ground. She is already leaving it. White tunic, blue mantle, hair loose, hands crossed, eyes lifted. A thin crescent moon cuts the lower edge. Seraphim crowd the sides. This is not an argument about doctrine. It is Seville’s answer to an invisible idea: purity made visible as light, cloth, and a face that still looks human while it rises. Bartolomé Esteban Murillo (Seville, 1617–1682) almost never left his city. After Zurbarán’s severity, he became the painter of grace — warm flesh, dissolving edges, theology that feels like weather. Spain already treated the Immaculate Conception as identity, not theory. Murillo painted it some twenty times. This small Prado canvas, from about 1665, is the formula at its most intimate: a girl of Seville lifted into air.
plaques.Q20270241: The Defense of Paris A dramatic depiction of the defense of Paris during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71. Meissonier captures the chaos and determination of the French forces, with soldiers and civilians gathered amid the devastated landscape. Rather than glorifying a single heroic figure, the painting emphasizes the collective struggle and desperation of a city under siege. Meissonier was deeply affected by the Franco-Prussian War and personally served in the National Guard during the defense of Paris. This gave the painting a personal connection that went beyond historical observation. He began the work soon after the conflict, using his own experiences and observations to portray the exhaustion, destruction, and patriotic resolve he had witnessed.
plaques.Q1087247: Jesus Returning the Keys to St. Peter (1820) Christ is shown handing the keys of Heaven to St. Peter, a scene drawn from the Gospel of Matthew. Ingres presents the moment with solemn simplicity, surrounding Christ and Peter with the Apostles. The carefully arranged figures, restrained gestures, and smooth, precise forms reflect the idealized beauty of Neoclassical painting. Ingres painted the work while in Italy, where he was deeply influenced by the art of the Renaissance, particularly the works of Raphael. The painting was commissioned for the church of Santissima Trinità dei Monti in Rome and reflects Ingres's admiration for religious art of the past. His deliberate composition and polished figures reveal his belief that painting should convey beauty, order, and timeless spiritual ideals rather than simply record reality.
plaques.Q18599519: The Holy Family — Jan van den Hoecke, c. 1630 Mary gently cradles the infant Christ while Joseph watches over them, creating an intimate scene of quiet tenderness. The warm light, rich colours, and softly idealised figures give the painting the dignified beauty characteristic of Flemish Baroque art, while the simplicity of the moment keeps the focus on the family itself. Van den Hoecke painted the Holy Family early in his career, drawing on the influence of Peter Paul Rubens and the grand tradition of Flemish religious painting. Rather than portraying a dramatic biblical event, he chose a private moment of affection and devotion, inviting the viewer to contemplate Christ not only as a divine figure, but as a child surrounded by the care of his family.
plaques.Q26767131: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa Francisco de Paula Van Halen (1864) Van Halen painted the scene more than six centuries after the battle, during a period when Spanish artists were increasingly drawn to important episodes from the nation’s medieval past. By portraying one of the major Christian victories of the Reconquista on a monumental scale, he transformed a historical event into a dramatic image of Spain’s medieval military history and heritage.
plaques.Q18177508: Springtime of Life Painted in 1871, near the end of the artist’s life, the work reflects Corot’s late fascination with poetic figure studies set within dreamlike landscapes. Rather than offering a specific portrait or narrative, he treats the young woman as an embodiment of youth and spring itself, allowing a gentle, melancholic mood to emerge from the harmonious blending of figure and nature.
plaques.Q19912776: The Farrier A blacksmith’s shop stands at the water’s edge, its forge and a nearby fire throwing warm light across figures, horses, and the darkened bank. Van der Neer fills the landscape with contrasting illumination, setting the orange glow of human labor against the cool moonlight and its reflections on the river, while a wooded shore rises quietly on the opposite side.
plaques.Q28035491: Archduke Ernest of Austria Alonso Sánchez Coello · 1568 Coello painted the portrait while Ernest was still a child, as part of the Habsburg court’s tradition of commissioning portraits of royal and aristocratic family members. Such works served not only as records of appearance, but also as visual representations of dynastic status and political connections. Coello’s refined style, influenced by the court portraiture of Titian and the Spanish Habsburg tradition, helped establish him as one of the leading portrait painters of the Spanish court.
plaques.Q28798007: The Shop Luis Paret y Alcázar · 1772 Paret painted scenes such as this to capture the character and customs of contemporary Spanish life rather than grand historical or religious subjects. His interest in ordinary people, interiors, and moments of daily activity reflects the influence of Rococo and European genre painting. The work demonstrates his ability to transform an everyday setting into an elegant and engaging glimpse of life in his time.
plaques.Q17322657: The Card Game on the Cradle: Allegory Johannes van Wijckersloot · c. 1650 · Dutch Painted around 1650 during the Dutch Golden Age, the work reflects the period’s fascination with genre scenes that concealed moral or symbolic messages beneath everyday activities. Van Wijckersloot used the card game and cradle as visual devices to explore themes of chance, childhood, and the passage of life, combining the observational character of Dutch genre painting with allegorical meaning.
plaques.Q27749025: The Judgement of Paris Francesco Albani · c. 1650 · Italian Francesco Albani’s The Judgement of Paris depicts the mythological moment when Paris, a Trojan prince, is asked to choose the most beautiful of three goddesses: Juno, Minerva, and Venus. The figures are presented in an idyllic landscape, surrounded by graceful poses and delicate details characteristic of Albani’s elegant style. Albani painted the subject as part of his fascination with classical mythology, a popular source of inspiration for Italian artists. The story allowed him to combine idealised beauty, mythology, and landscape while exploring themes of love, beauty, and divine rivalry. His soft colours and graceful figures reflect the refined, lyrical character of his mature work.
plaques.Q2888251: The Battle of Cassel on 23rd August 1328 Hendrik Scheffer · 1837 · Dutch-French The Battle of Cassel on 23rd August 1328 depicts the decisive clash between the forces of King Philip VI of France and the Flemish rebels led by Nicolaas Zannekin. Soldiers and cavalrymen meet in a violent struggle, with the crowded battlefield and dramatic movement conveying the intensity of the medieval conflict. Scheffer painted the scene more than five centuries after the battle, during the 19th-century revival of interest in dramatic episodes from European history. The subject allowed him to combine historical storytelling with the emotional and theatrical style of Romanticism, bringing a distant medieval event vividly to life for contemporary viewers.
plaques.Q28019036: The Siege of Presnitz, 1641 Peter Snayers · 1648 · Flemish Snayers was renowned for his detailed depictions of military campaigns, often creating large panoramic compositions that documented battles and sieges with remarkable precision. Painted only a few years after the event, this work reflects his close association with military subjects and his interest in recording the movements, formations, and landscapes of warfare during the Thirty Years’ War.
plaques.Q89031249: Scene in a Brothel with the Holy Family on the Flight into Egypt Gillis Mostaert · c. 1550 · Flemish Gillis Mostaert combines a biblical story with a striking scene of everyday life. In the foreground, figures gather in the lively interior of a brothel, while the Holy Family’s Flight into Egypt appears within the composition, creating a deliberate contrast between sacred and worldly subjects. The crowded setting and numerous small details reflect Mostaert’s skill in depicting the activities and character of ordinary life. Mostaert was particularly interested in scenes that blended religious narratives with contemporary settings and human behaviour. By placing the Holy Family alongside a morally charged environment, he created a contrast between Christian virtue and worldly temptation, a theme that would have resonated strongly with 16th-century viewers. The work demonstrates the Northern Renaissance tradition of embedding religious meaning within detailed scenes of everyday life.
plaques.Q139620147: The Oldest Sister, a Souvenir from Brittany François-Alfred Delobbe · 1879 · French Delobbe was drawn to scenes of rural life and frequently travelled to Brittany, where he found inspiration in its landscapes, people, and traditional customs. Painted in 1879, the work reflects the 19th-century French fascination with regional identity and picturesque rural communities. Rather than depicting a grand historical event, Delobbe transforms an ordinary person into a lasting portrait of Breton life and culture.
plaques.Q84448006: Yael Kills Sisera Gregorio Lazzarini · c. 1650 · Italian The subject comes from the Book of Judges and was a popular theme among European artists because it combined violence, courage, and divine deliverance. Lazzarini used the episode to explore the dramatic possibilities of biblical history, presenting Yael as both a determined heroine and the central figure of the composition. His theatrical approach reflects the influence of the Baroque tradition of using powerful gestures and emotionally charged moments to engage the viewer.
plaques.Q58191898: Saint Bruno, Founder of the Carthusian Order Jan de Hoey (1545–1615)
plaques.Q17524144: Kenau Fighting in Defense of Haarlem Barend Wijnveld · 1854 · Dutch Barend Wijnveld’s Kenau Fighting in Defense of Haarlem depicts the legendary Kenau Simonsdochter Hasselaer taking part in the defense of Haarlem during the Spanish siege of 1572–1573. She is shown amid the fighting, surrounded by soldiers and the chaos of battle, presenting her as a symbol of courage and resistance. Wijnveld painted the scene centuries after the siege, during the 19th-century revival of interest in Dutch history and national heroes. Kenau had become a celebrated figure in Dutch historical tradition, and the subject allowed Wijnveld to combine patriotic history with the dramatic, emotional style of Romantic-era history painting. The painting is therefore less a literal record of the siege than a 19th-century interpretation of a celebrated episode from Dutch history.
plaques.Q59825736: The Battle of Aljubarrota Mariano Salvador Maella · 1791 · Spanish Maella painted the scene more than four centuries after the battle, drawing on an important episode in Portuguese and Iberian history. The subject allowed him to transform a celebrated medieval victory into a grand historical composition, reflecting the 18th-century interest in depicting significant events from the past with dramatic storytelling, idealised figures, and strong emotional contrasts.
plaques.Q119808148: A Naval Battle between Christian and Turkish Ships Cornelis de Wael · c. 1650 · Flemish De Wael was particularly known for paintings of battles and military life, drawing on his experience and interest in Mediterranean scenes. The conflict between Christian and Ottoman forces was a recurring subject in 17th-century European art, reflecting ongoing political and religious tensions in the Mediterranean. His dramatic treatment of ships, movement, and atmosphere reflects the Flemish tradition of detailed battle painting.
plaques.Q28466203: The Massacre of the Innocents Daniele da Volterra · 1557 · Italian Daniele da Volterra’s The Massacre of the Innocents depicts the biblical slaughter of children ordered by King Herod following the birth of Christ. Soldiers move violently through a crowded scene as mothers desperately attempt to protect their children. The twisting poses, expressive gestures, and tightly packed figures create a powerful sense of anguish and turmoil. The subject comes from the Gospel of Matthew and was frequently depicted by Renaissance artists for its dramatic emotional possibilities. Painted in 1557, the work reflects Daniele’s close engagement with the monumental style of Michelangelo, whose influence can be seen in the muscular figures, complex poses, and dramatic composition. The painting combines the religious narrative with the heightened physicality and emotional intensity characteristic of late Italian Mannerism.
plaques.Q27180395: The Cardsharps Valentin de Boulogne French, 1591–1632 c. 1615–18 Oil on canvas 94.5 × 137 cm Valentin de Boulogne was among the most gifted of the French Caravaggisti working in Rome. This early masterpiece adapts Caravaggio’s celebrated Cardsharps into a darker, more psychologically charged tavern scene. A young, unsuspecting player is being cheated by two confederates: one hides extra cards behind his back while the other, lurking in shadow, reads the victim’s hand and signals the information.
plaques.Q17325393: Church Interior with Christ Preaching to a Crowd Attributed to Cornelis van Dalem and Jan van Wechelen Flemish, c. 1528–1573 / c. 1530–1570 c. 1545–1570 Oil on panel 58.8 × 92.7 cm Christ sits among a contemporary crowd inside a spacious but sparsely decorated Gothic church and preaches. In the foreground Catholic clergymen chase children away. The architecture is rendered with careful perspective; the figures, probably by Jan van Wechelen, introduce everyday incidents—beggars, dogs, a flirting couple—that keep the scene grounded in 16th-century life. Van Dalem, a landscape painter of humanist education who was suspected of Protestant leanings, may have intended a pointed comparison between Christ’s direct teaching and the practices of the Catholic Church of his own day. The almost empty interior also belongs to the moment after the iconoclastic riots of 1566, when the proper appearance and purpose of a church were fiercely debated.
plaques.Q27781243: Sancho Panza recovers his lost donkey José Moreno Carbonero Spanish, Málaga 1860–Madrid 1942 c. 1894 Sancho Panza, reunited with the donkey stolen from him on the road, embraces and kisses the animal “as if it were a human being.” The scene follows chapter 30 of the first part of Don Quixote. Around them stand the other figures from the episode—Dorotea, Don Quixote, the priest, Cardenio, and the barber—on a dusty La Mancha highway under full midday sun. Moreno Carbonero was among the last major Spanish history painters. After a stay in Paris in 1877 he returned repeatedly to Cervantes, treating the novel with the same archaeological exactness he brought to large historical machines. Shown at the National Exhibition of Fine Arts in 1895, the picture was praised for its “photographic” naturalism and for a road that critics recognized as unmistakably manchego. In an age that looked back to the Golden Age for a national identity, Sancho’s homely tenderness toward his rucio was as Spanish a subject as Don Quixote’s madness.
plaques.Q18572318: Summer (L’Été) Giuseppe Arcimboldo Italian, Milan c. 1526/27–1593 1573 Oil on canvas 76 × 64 cm Musée du Louvre, Paris (RF 1964-31) A profile bust composed of the fruits, vegetables, and grains of high summer. A peach forms the cheek, a cucumber the nose, cherries the lip, an eggplant the ear, wheat the eyebrow; the garment is woven straw, with an artichoke at the breast. The artist signed and dated the painting in the wheat of the collar and sleeve: GIUSEPPE ARCIMBOLDO F 1573. This canvas belongs to the only complete surviving set of Arcimboldo’s Four Seasons, painted in 1573 for Emperor Maximilian II as a gift to Augustus of Saxony. It repeats, with small changes, a composition Arcimboldo had invented in 1563. At the Habsburg court such “composite heads” were admired as learned jokes: nature made to impersonate a human face, the seasons made to impersonate the ages of man, and imperial order made visible in the harmony of the harvest.
plaques.Q27020819: The Draughtsmen c. 1870–80 Henriëtte Ronner-Knip Dutch–Belgian, 1821–1909 Oil on panel 43.7 × 65.3 cm A group of kittens has taken over an artist’s studio. One paws at paper or canvas as if drawing; others inspect brushes, sketches, and studio clutter with the solemn concentration of professionals and the restlessness of cats. The joke is gentle but precise: the animals behave like draughtsmen while remaining unmistakably themselves. Ronner-Knip was born in Amsterdam into a family of painters and trained by her father, Josephus Augustus Knip. After her marriage in 1850 she settled in Brussels, first making her name with dogs—working animals and fashionable lapdogs alike—then, from about 1870, turning almost exclusively to cats. By then the long-haired salon cat had become a bourgeois status object; her pictures of them in richly furnished interiors sold widely across Europe and America. She posed her models in a purpose-built glass enclosure, using cushions and paper sculptures to hold the animals in the required attitudes before transferring the scene to panel. The result is both anecdotal and closely observed. Texture of fur, sheen of fabric, and the particular psychology of each kitten are rendered with the same care she once gave to Brabant livestock. Critics later dismissed the work as merely charming; contemporaries did not. She received the Order of Leopold in 1887 and the Order of Orange-Nassau in 1901, rare honours for a woman artist of her generation. The Draughtsmen belongs to the moment when her commercial success and her eye for feline character were at their height.
plaques.Q28808973: St Kilda Park c. 1880 Louis Buvelot Switzerland/Australia, 1814–1888 Oil on paper, laid on cardboard 56.0 × 71.0 cm
plaques.Q25388274: Leonardo da Cutro and Ruy López Play Chess at the Spanish Court Luigi Mussini (Italian, 1813–1888) 1883 Oil on canvas 30 3/8 × 52 3/8 in. (77 × 133 cm) In a marble hall of Philip II’s court, the Calabrian master Giovanni Leonardo Di Bona—called Il Puttino, “the little one”—rises from the board and opens his arms. Opposite him, the Spanish priest and theorist Ruy López de Segura, author of the 1561 treatise that gave its name to the Ruy Lopez opening, slumps over the pieces. The king watches from his chair; courtiers, confessors, and hunting dogs fill the rest of the room. The scene commemorates the Madrid contest of 1575, often cited as the first documented international chess tournament. Fifteen years earlier López had beaten Leonardo in Rome. Tradition holds that at court the Italian lost the first two games, then won the next three, and asked that his prize—a thousand ducats—be converted into twenty years of tax relief and city status for his hometown of Cutro. Later chroniclers embroidered the episode; Mussini painted the legend at its most theatrical moment: checkmate announced before the throne. Mussini, director of the Accademia di Belle Arti in Siena and himself a published chess-problem composer, treated the match as history painting in the Purist manner: exact costume, measured light from a high window, and every jewel and fresco described with academic patience. The canvas was discussed more in European chess journals than in art reviews—exactly the audience, Mussini admitted, for whom he had made it.
plaques.Q119795456: White Goats Giuseppe Palizzi Italian, 1812–1888 Oil on canvas, c. 1845–1869 31.2 × 45 cm Palizzi was a specialist in animals and rural scenes. After training in Naples he settled in Paris in 1844 and became one of the first Italian painters to work in the Forest of Fontainebleau with the Barbizon School. He was particularly admired for his goats, which he painted from many angles and with a close attention to light on their coats. Here five white goats occupy a rocky hillside under a divided sky. On the left three animals stand alert against dark rocks and a threatening cloud; one looks upward with its mouth open. On the right two others rest in calmer light before a distant landscape. The contrast of mood, the luminous whites and greys of the fur, and the loose handling of paint are typical of Palizzi’s mature style.
plaques.Q119702041: Sergeant Luke O’Connor Winning His VC at the Battle of the Alma, 20th September 1854 Louis William Desanges English, 1822–1905 Oil on canvas, c. 1858–1860 65 × 78 cm Desanges was a London portraitist of French descent. In 1858, while painting the Crimean veteran Robert Lindsay, he conceived a series of pictures showing Victoria Cross winners at the moment of their actions. Some fifty canvases were completed by 1862 and exhibited at the Egyptian Hall and the Crystal Palace. Here Sergeant Luke O’Connor of the 23rd Regiment, already wounded in the breast, seizes the fallen Queen’s Colour and carries it forward. Desanges places him at the centre beneath the flag, with comrades, smoke and the slope of the Alma behind him.
plaques.Q131688786: Battle of Aboukir Louis-François, Baron Lejeune French, 1775–1848 Oil on canvas, 1804 185 × 255 cm French infantry and cavalry drive the Ottoman army back toward the sea on the peninsula of Aboukir, 25 July 1799. Bonaparte and Berthier watch from horseback at the left; combats, camels, fallen men and the Mediterranean fill the rest of the field. The action is spread across the canvas rather than gathered around a single heroic charge. Lejeune was an engineer officer and aide-de-camp to Marshal Berthier. He painted the battles of the Empire from sketches and official accounts; he had not served in Egypt. This canvas was one of three he showed at the Salon of 1804.
plaques.Q51756376: Charles the Bold found after the Battle of Nancy Auguste Feyen-Perrin French, 1826–1888 Oil on canvas, 1865 200.5 × 304.5 cm Two days after the Battle of Nancy, the stripped body of Charles the Bold lies by a frozen pool. Companions kneel around the nude corpse and identify him by his ring and the long nails of his hand. Feyen-Perrin stages the discovery as a secular Pietà: the pale academic nude at the centre, winter ground, a horse and dark trees behind. Born at Bey-sur-Seille in Lorraine, Feyen-Perrin studied in Nancy and in Paris under Cogniet and Yvon. He showed at the Salon from 1853 and won a medal in 1865, the year of this canvas. Later known for Breton fisherwomen at Cancale, he treated this local history subject on a large scale; the State deposited the picture in Nancy the same year. Signed lower left: A. Feyen-Perrin.Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nancy
plaques.Q106610747: King Murat presenting an award to the Cérès, 1809 Guillaume Descamps French, 1779–1858 Oil on canvas, 1809 105 × 43 cm On the deck of the Neapolitan frigate Cérès, Joachim Murat rewards the crew after the fight of 27 June 1809 in the Gulf of Naples. The king presents decorations; Captain Giovanni Bausan is made commander of the Order of the Two Sicilies. Wounded sailors, officers and flags fill the tall, narrow canvas, with the gulf beyond. Descamps, a pupil of François-André Vincent, won the second Prix de Rome in 1802 and became court painter to Murat at Naples. He treated this official ceremony as history painting and later engraved the composition himself.
plaques.Q50862885: The Death of Nelson at the Battle of Trafalgar, 21 October 1805 Samuel Drummond British, 1765–1844 Oil on canvas, 1806 72.5 × 82.5 cm Nelson, struck at about 1.30 p.m. by a musket ball from the French Redoutable, is carried below so the men will not lose heart. Two sailors and a marine support him down the companionway. A dead marine, an injured sailor, a musket and a discarded hat lie on the deck; beyond, the fight continues in smoke and sails. The grouping recalls a Deposition from the Cross. Drummond served at sea as a youth before entering the Royal Academy Schools in 1791 and becoming an Associate in 1808. He painted this subject in many versions from 1806 to 1828; a large canvas was shown at the British Institution in 1807.
plaques.Q18549884: Leaving Home reminds us all of the heartache and fear a family has as it sends a loved one off to war. Here the father bravely wishes his son well as those near and dear to him gather round. The model for the young boy leaving for the war was Dan Tanton who attended church with Gilbert Gaul. The model for the father depicted in this painting was a Confederate veteran who lived in Nashville at the time. The two daughters were painted from the same model, Mary LeSeur.
plaques.Q18533319: One northern artist who often represented the Confederate emblems was Gilbert Gaul. Gaul was only ten years old at the end of the war. During the first fifteen years of his career, he almost exclusively painted scenes from the Civil War, and, even if he was from a Unionist family from the state of New Jersey, he most often chose to depict southern soldiers.
